title: Check what an item demands, not its tag
statement: Check, item by item rather than from tags or averages, that each item and lesson actually demands the skill, standard, topic and passage its labels claim.
example: One grade 3 course needed 193 items retagged for systematic mistags.
detail: One grade 3 reading course had systematic standard mistags, vocabulary in context on the wrong standard and comprehension on the wrong strand, and 193 items were retagged; the generator's rubric now audits tags and reports an error rate (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/course-formula-agents.md`). After a retag counted as successful, a main-idea lesson still served an inference item, so the check is the skill claimed against the skill assessed, item by item (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/course-red-team/references/finding-taxonomy.md`), and the course-plan standard calls such a lesson a tagging and a teaching defect (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/instruction-quality-standard.md`). Tag coverage is plumbing, never the curriculum claim (the same file), and the grade 3 criteria ask that every standard map to at least one knowledge component, with no orphans and no false alignment, where an item matches a standard's vocabulary but its depth of knowledge is lower (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D7-knowledge-first-curriculum.md`). Make the item-by-item check a blocking check of its own. Where a lesson's items do not demand the skill it claims to teach, fix the content rather than the tag, since a retagged item can fit its new tag and still break the lesson.
against: Lenient by design: 'A lesson where items plausibly fit their tags PASSES.' (`shadow-bench/src/inceptbench/prompts/lesson_bundle/evaluation.txt`, line 13).

evidence.quote: A lesson's items must assess the KC the lesson claims to teach (construct coherence — a main-idea lesson serving inference items is a tagging *and* teaching defect).

Tagging still does not match what items assess. A main-idea lesson served an "Inference & Evidence" item, and single short passages carry several different question types, so the standard a lesson claims to teach and the items it delivers do not line up.
A superficially valid stimulus can teach or assess the wrong construct.
